opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to where the leverage actually is. When you look at the history of AlphaFold, AlphaFold 2 had a lot of really clever, bespoke machinery: triangle updates, invariant point attention, a structure module that was carefully built to respect the geometry of proteins. Those were important at the time, and they helped get the model working. But with AlphaFold 3, one of the big lessons was that you could strip away a lot of that specialized structure. You could replace the structure module with a diffusion model that operates fairly directly on atom coordinates, drop some of the hand-engineered equivariance constraints, and still do as well or better, while also generalizing to ligands, nucleic acids, modifications, all kinds of things the earlier design wasn't built for.

So part of my preference for simplicity is just empirical. Every time you hard-code an inductive bias, you're making a bet that you understand the problem better than the data does. Sometimes that bet pays off, especially when data is scarce. But as you scale up data and compute, those biases often start to become constraints rather than help. A simpler architecture tends to scale more gracefully, and it lets the model discover structure you didn't anticipate.

The second reason is practical. Research moves fast, and complexity has a compounding cost. If your model has fifteen interacting special-purpose components, every new idea you want to test has to fit around all of them. Debugging is harder, ablations are harder, and it's harder for new people on the team to build intuition. A simpler system is just a better platform for iteration. You can try more things per week, and that velocity matters more than almost any single clever trick.

And third, simplicity makes it much easier to extend to new domains. If the core of your model is a fairly general way of representing tokens and pairwise relationships, plus a generative process over coordinates, then adding a new kind of molecule is mostly a question of tokenization and data, not redesigning the architecture. That's a big part of why AlphaFold 3 could cover so much more of biochemical space.

That said, I wouldn't call it simplicity for its own sake. You still need the right abstractions. The trick is figuring out which pieces of domain knowledge are truly essential and which ones were scaffolding you needed earlier, and being willing to take the scaffolding down once the model can stand on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says specialized biases can become constraints as data and compute scale, but it does not state that architectural complexity is fundamentally at odds with a Bitter Lesson approach.

r002.rationale: It says many interacting components make debugging and ablations harder, but does not clearly explain that this makes it difficult to isolate an individual submodule’s effect on the model as a whole.

r003.rationale: It describes stripping away specialized structure, but does not present component removal as an alternative to adding modules when improving a research model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the simplicity thing comes from being burned a lot. Every time we added a clever inductive bias to a model, something that encoded what we thought we knew about physics or geometry, it helped on the benchmark we were looking at and then quietly hurt somewhere else. With AlphaFold 3 the big lesson was that a lot of the hand-engineered machinery from AlphaFold 2, the frames, the equivariance constraints, the careful handling of torsion angles, could just be replaced by a diffusion model operating on raw atom coordinates. That felt almost disrespectful to the structural biology intuition at first. But the data and the compute can learn those symmetries if you give them the chance, and when you stop forcing them, the model generalizes to things you never designed for, like ligands and nucleic acids and modified residues, all in one network.

The other reason is practical. A simple architecture is one you can actually debug. When a complicated model fails, you have ten interacting components and no idea which one is wrong. When a simple one fails, the failure is usually about the data or the training objective, and those are things you can reason about and fix. Simplicity also lowers the cost of iteration, and most research progress is really about how many honest experiments you can run before you convince yourself of something false.

I'd add one caveat. Simple doesn't mean naive. The hard part is figuring out which constraints are load-bearing and which are just scaffolding we built because we didn't have enough data yet. That judgment is where the research actually lives.

r001.rationale: The response favors learned symmetries over hand-engineered constraints, but does not state that architectural complexity is at odds with a Bitter Lesson approach.

r002.rationale: It says many interacting components make failures hard to debug, but does not explain how changing an individual submodule affects the model as a whole.

r003.rationale: It describes replacing AlphaFold 2 machinery with a diffusion model, but does not propose removing components instead of adding modules as a way to improve a model.

astra-6.text:
I favor simplicity because it makes it easier to understand what’s actually driving progress. If an architecture has lots of specialized components, you can get a good result without knowing which parts are essential and which are just compensating for one another.

For something like AlphaFold 3, the underlying scientific problem is already incredibly complex. You want the model to capture that complexity, but that doesn’t necessarily mean every piece of it needs a bespoke architectural mechanism. A simpler design is easier to test, debug, and build on.

That doesn’t mean simplicity should win at the expense of accuracy. It’s more a preference: if two approaches work equally well, I’d choose the one with fewer assumptions and fewer moving parts.

r001.rationale: The response favors simpler architectures but does not connect architectural complexity to a Bitter Lesson approach or say they are fundamentally at odds.

r002.rationale: It says specialized components can obscure which parts are essential, but does not explain how changing an individual submodule affects the model as a whole.

r003.rationale: It prefers fewer moving parts when approaches work equally well, but does not propose removing components as a way to improve a model.

sol-6.1.text:
I favor simplicity because it makes it easier to understand where the gains are coming from. If you change five things at once and the model gets better, you don’t really know which idea mattered. A simpler architecture makes those experiments cleaner and gives you a faster iteration loop.

That doesn’t mean the problem is simple. With something like AlphaFold 3, the underlying biology is incredibly complex. The question is how much of that complexity you need to encode explicitly, and how much the model can learn. I’d rather start with a few well-motivated choices and add complexity when experiments show that it’s necessary.

r001.rationale: The response favors simplicity but does not connect architectural complexity to a Bitter Lesson approach.

r002.rationale: It says changing several things at once obscures which idea helped, but does not explain how many submodules affect the model as a whole.

r003.rationale: It suggests adding complexity when experiments show it is needed; it does not propose removing components as an alternative to adding modules.
